lines.text: Wavelength or frequency of light from a transition on an energy-level diagram → photon energy = the gap between the two levels, converted to J, then $\lambda = \frac{hc}{\Delta E}$; the smallest gap gives the longest wavelength ({{lesson:5.2}})

Alpha particle fired head-on at a nucleus, how close it gets → energy conservation with the nucleus fixed: initial $E_\text{k}$ = electric $E_\text{p}$ at rest, so $d = \frac{2kZe^{2}}{E_\text{k}}$ with $E_\text{k}$ in J ({{lesson:5.3}})

Light on a metal, a stopping potential or a graph of $E_\text{max}$ against $f$ → $E_\text{max} = hf - \Phi = eV_\text{s}$, with every energy in the same unit; on the graph, gradient $h$ and frequency intercept $f_0$ ({{lesson:5.4}})

Wavelength of a moving electron or other particle, or electron diffraction rings → $\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$; well below $c$, $p = mv = \sqrt{2mE_\text{k}}$, with $E_\text{k} = eV$ in J for an accelerated electron ({{lesson:5.5}})

X-ray or gamma photon scattered by an electron through an angle → $\Delta\lambda = \frac{h}{m_\text{e}c}(1 - \cos\theta)$ with $\theta$ the photon's angle; the electron's kinetic energy is the energy the photon lost ({{lesson:5.5}})

Energy released by a fission, fusion or decay, given masses → mass before − mass after, counting every neutron, electron and positron; masses in u × 931.5 give MeV, masses in kg use $\Delta E = \Delta m\, c^{2}$ for J ({{lesson:5.6}})

Energy released, given binding energies per nucleon → total binding energy $= A \times \frac{E_\text{B}}{A}$ for each nucleus; energy released = total after − total before, with free neutrons and protons counting zero ({{lesson:5.6}})

Count rate after a whole number of half-lives, with a background reading → subtract the background, multiply by $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n}$ with $n = \frac{t}{T_{\frac{1}{2}}}$, then add the background back if asked what the counter reads ({{lesson:5.8}})

Nuclei or activity left after any time, or a half-life from a decay constant → $N = N_0\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda t}$ with $\lambda$ and $t$ in the same unit, $A = \lambda N$ with $\lambda$ in $\text{s}^{-1}$ for Bq, and $T_{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$ ({{lesson:5.10}})

Maximum kinetic energy of beta particles from masses → $E_\text{max} \approx \Delta m\, c^{2}$ with $\Delta m = M_\text{parent} - M_\text{daughter} - m_\text{e}$ for nuclear masses; at $E_\text{max}$ the (anti)neutrino gets almost nothing ({{lesson:5.9}})

Fuel used each second by a star or a power station → reactions per second = power from the reactions ÷ energy per reaction in J (the star's luminosity, or the plant's electrical output ÷ efficiency), then × mass used per reaction ({{lesson:5.12}})

Radius of a star from parallax, apparent brightness and peak wavelength → $d = \frac{1}{p}$ in pc, converted to m; $L = 4\pi d^{2}b$; $T$ from Wien's law; then $R = \sqrt{\frac{L}{4\pi\sigma T^{4}}}$, or $\frac{R}{R_\odot} = \sqrt{\frac{L}{L_\odot}}\left(\frac{T_\odot}{T}\right)^{2}$ for ratios ({{lesson:5.13}})
